newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambians vote despite opposition call for boycott.
newsitem.headline: Zambians vote despite opposition call for boycott.

text.p: Zambia voted on Monday despite a boycott by the main opposition and pressure from Western countries who fear the election is largely a cosmetic show of democracy.

President Frederick Chiluba is set for a second term after barring a challenge from his only strong rival, "Father of the Nation" Kenneth Kaunda, whom he beat in the first free elections in 1991 on a free-market and democracy platform.

Enraged at the bar on Kaunda running, the former president's United National Independence Party (UNIP) walked out of parliament and led a seven-party boycott of the presidential and parliamentary polls they call a farce.
UNIP is hoping for a dismal turnout, but state officials said it was brisk despite downpours and a flawed registration system that has left out half of the 4.6 million adults.
"Voters in their numbers are throwing election boycotts to the wind," state radio said.
"It is quite fine, voter turnout is excellent after a poor start due to rains," an electoral commission spokesman said.
Polls close at five p.m. (1500 GMT) and final results are expected on Tuesday or Wednesday.
Chiluba, 53, voted in his Copperbelt region stronghold and Kaunda, 72, went to play his favourite sport, golf.
Kaunda was blocked from running under a new constitution passed in May by Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian-born.
Kaunda, who led Zambia to independence from Britain in 1964 and founded a one-party state on African-Christian-socialist "humanism", said he would call for the results to be annulled.
Police said they had no reports of the feared violence or rioting. But whatever the outcome of the vote, political strife and economic hardship are set to intensify.
UNIP launched a campaign of civil disobedience and predicted Chiluba's downfall within six months, assuming he beats his four remaining challengers.
Foreign donors, upset by the bar on Kaunda and other political developments in what had been a model of African progress, have frozen aid to help Zambia cope with its $6.4 billion external debt.
"Many of the hard-won gains of the last five years of reform are now at risk from the donor freeze," said the Standard Chartered bank group's September report on Zambia.
The World Bank says privatisation and economic reform in Zambia -- rich in copper but impoverished -- are second to none in Africa.

After the vote donors will face a dilemma -- to watch Zambia's economic promise fade or back down and resume aid after failing, like South African President Nelson Mandela, to make Chiluba reopen dialogue with UNIP.
The Kaunda affair has dominated the campaign and diplomats said the main parties now differ little on policy.
Chiluba, who humiliated Kaunda by winning 125 out of 150 seats in 1991, reminded voters of the bad old days of economic ruin, secret police and no democracy.
Kaunda, set to forfeit UNIP's 25 seats, appealed to the poor who are 12 percent worse off in real terms now than in 1991 and to whom restructuring has brought scant material benefit.
